Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette:
Clara was eight years old the first time she watched her father’s hand close into a fist and swing across the kitchen table into her mother’s cheekbone. The thud—dull, wet—stayed in her ears. She remembered the way her mother’s head snapped sideways, the way the coffee cup tipped and rolled off the tablecloth. But after that, nothing. She could not recall whether her mother fell, whether her father said anything, whether she herself had screamed or run. For years she tried to fill that blank, but the memory simply stopped, mid-frame, like a tape cut short. What remained was the frozen feeling in her body: arms pressed to her sides, shoulders locked, feet glued to the linoleum just inside the kitchen doorway. Even now, thirty years later, when a memory surfaced, her whole frame would stiffen into that exact child’s stance, as if her muscles remembered what her mind could not.

Clara became a city council member because she believed in order, in rules that kept people safe. But the council chamber had become a place of hidden threats. During debates over zoning amendments, she would watch the other members’ hands—the way a fist tightened on a pen, the way an index finger stabbed the air. She watched their jawlines for the first sign of a clench. A raised voice from the public gallery sent her pulse into her throat; a sudden chair scrape made her flinch. She had come to believe that danger lived in ordinary anger, that any conflict might bleed into violence, and that she alone was responsible for spotting it. The only places she felt even close to safe were her locked office with its solid door and the quiet of her own living room after her husband had gone to bed. Even there, sleep came slowly. She lay in the dark, listening for footsteps, for a voice with an edge, her body bracing for something she could not name.

The memory of that kitchen was rarely far. A harsh word from a constituent would send it rising—the damp sound, the stillness, the blank after. And the memory, once triggered, made the watching worse. The more she remembered, the more certain she became that she could not let her guard down. She would scan the council chamber again, cataloging every exit, every potential threat, her chest tight. The cycle tightened over months. The more she watched, the more hypervigilant she became, and that hypervigilance itself triggered pieces of the memory—a flash of her mother’s eyes, the smell of burnt coffee, the feeling of her own small body locked in place. She could not break the loop.

At work, Clara began avoiding certain meetings. She delegated a contentious public safety committee to her deputy, telling herself it was strategic. When colleagues pressed her to attend, she made excuses—too much casework, a headache. Inside, she was certain that if she sat in that room with raised voices, she would either freeze or flee, and then everyone would see. The avoidance cost her a vote on a measure she had championed; she felt a quiet shame but could not persuade herself to return.

What finally brought Clara to the clinic was a Tuesday afternoon during a transportation planning hearing. A man in the audience stood and shouted that the council was wasting tax dollars. His voice was loud, not violent, but something in its pitch—the frustration, the sudden break in harmony—pinned her to her chair. Her arms went stiff at her sides. She could not speak for the next three minutes. When she drove home that evening, she stared at her hands on the steering wheel and thought: *This is not going to stop on its own.* She was afraid of what her colleagues would think if they knew, afraid that her husband would see her as fragile. But more than that, she was tired of the small world she had built around safe rooms and locked doors. She wanted to believe that a city council chamber could hold a heated argument without turning into a kitchen. She wanted her body to unclench.
